# Results — Study 933 (Same Issuer, Two Ladders) on the real daily tape

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Eight issuers that list **both**
a perpetual **preferred** and an exchange-traded **baby bond** ($25-par notes) are held as two
equal-weight ladders, rebalanced monthly with **one execution lag** (weights set from the
month-end state through day `t`, applied from `t+1`), **25 bps one-way cost** (a PROXY,
swept below), both measured **excess-of-cash** (minus BIL's total return). Daily
**total-return** closes (`yfinance`, `auto_adjust=True`) — price-only would be meaningless
between two coupon instruments. Common window **2022-02-02 → 2026-06-30**, gated by the last
pair leg to list (OXLCZ / BIPI, January 2022). As-of **2026-06-30** (the partial current
month is dropped).*

## Data stamp

| Legs | Window | n days | Fingerprint |
|---|---|---|---|
| 8 preferreds + 8 baby bonds (16 legs) | 2022-02-02 → 2026-06-30 | 1,105 | Fingerprint `9ae51d88019e` |

Cash leg **BIL**; sector benchmark **PFF**; cross-checks CMSA/CMSD/BEPI/BIPI (alternative
rungs) and SACH-PA/SACC/SCCB (a redeemed pair, for the survivorship probe) are cached too.

**The pairs.** CMS Energy (CMS-PB / CMSC), Duke Energy (DUK-PA / DUKB), Brookfield Renewable
(BEP-PA / BEPH), Brookfield Infrastructure (BIP-PA / BIPH), B. Riley Financial (RILYP /
RILYZ), Oxford Lane Capital (OXLCP / OXLCZ), Eagle Point Credit (ECC-PD / ECCC), Babcock &
Wilcox (BW-PA / BWNB). Each pair is **one balance sheet**: the same obligor, two listed rungs.

**But the rungs are not the same rungs twice over** (`data.RUNG_STRUCTURE`). The headline
framing — *junior perpetual preferred vs senior dated note* — is exact for only **two of the
eight** pairs:

| Pair | Junior rung | Senior rung | Step |
|---|---|---|---|
| CMS Energy | cumulative convertible preferred | **junior subordinated** notes 2078 | narrow |
| Duke Energy | perpetual preferred | **junior subordinated** debentures 2078 | narrow |
| Brookfield Renewable | perpetual preferred units | **perpetual** subordinated notes | narrow |
| Brookfield Infra. | perpetual preferred units | **perpetual** subordinated notes | narrow |
| B. Riley Financial | perpetual preferred | senior notes 2028 | **wide** |
| Oxford Lane Capital | **dated** term preferred 2027 | senior notes 2031 | narrow |
| Eagle Point Credit | **dated** term preferred 2031 | senior notes 2031 | narrow |
| Babcock & Wilcox | perpetual preferred | senior notes 2026 | **wide** |

In four pairs the "bond" is itself junior subordinated or perpetual; in two the "preferred"
is a dated, mandatorily redeemable term preferred. **A one-rung step cannot pay a two-rung
premium** — this heterogeneity is part of the answer, not a footnote to it, and it is why the
two *wide*-step pairs (B. Riley, Babcock & Wilcox) turn out to carry the entire result below.

## The two ladders — excess-of-cash

| Ladder | Excess Sharpe | CAGR | Vol | Max drawdown | HAC *t* (mean) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **Preferred (junior)** | **+0.368** | +5.35% | 18.96% | **−30.8%** | +0.68 |
| **Baby bond (senior)** | **+0.202** | +1.82% | 13.31% | **−20.4%** | +0.38 |

- **Excess-Sharpe advantage (preferred − bond): +0.166** — the right sign for a seniority
  premium, but the HAC *t* on the daily ladder return difference is only **+0.65**.
- **Pairwise, same-issuer spread: +3.10%/yr, HAC *t* = +0.55.** This is the headline
  estimator: because both legs are the *same* credit, the issuer's spread factor cancels and
  what is left is the price of seniority alone. It is a **statistical mean, not a portfolio** —
  an arithmetic average of daily percentage differences, which re-equal-weights the eight
  pairs every day and pays no cost. The *tradable* expressions are the monthly, costed ladder
  spread (**+4.29%/yr**) and the dollar-neutral long-short below.
- Panel vol ratio **1.42×** (excess-of-cash net baskets), ladder drawdown **−30.8% vs −20.4%**,
  and the preferred rung is the more volatile one in **6 of 8** pairs *at daily frequency* —
  but see **"Is the risk step a fact or a tape artefact?"** below, where 6/8 becomes **2/8** at
  monthly frequency and **0/6** once the two distressed issuers are removed.
- Annual turnover of a ladder is ~75%, so cost is small and near-symmetric across the arms.

## Bootstrap CIs (2,000 draws, 21-day blocks, arms resampled jointly)

| Quantity | Point | 95% CI | share < 0 |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| Preferred ladder excess Sharpe | +0.368 | [−0.736, +1.351] | 25.2% |
| Baby-bond ladder excess Sharpe | +0.202 | [−0.823, +1.256] | 35.2% |
| **Sharpe advantage (pref − bond)** | **+0.166** | **[−0.470, +0.804]** | 32.3% |
| **Pairwise spread (%/yr)** | **+3.10%** | **[−6.80%, +13.57%]** | — |

Every interval straddles zero by a wide margin. Four and a half years of eight correlated
pairs simply does not have the power to price seniority.

## Issuer by issuer — where the panel average comes from

| Issuer | Pref CAGR | Bond CAGR | Pref vol | Bond vol | Pref DD | Bond DD | Spread (HAC *t*) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| CMS Energy | −2.13% | +1.84% | 24.0% | 10.5% | −23.2% | −14.7% | **−1.64%** (−0.22) |
| Duke Energy | +3.82% | +3.05% | 9.5% | 9.6% | −13.1% | −12.6% | +0.73% (+0.24) |
| Brookfield Renewable | −3.33% | −3.74% | 23.2% | 22.4% | −32.9% | −37.7% | +0.62% (+0.07) |
| Brookfield Infra. | −1.15% | −2.54% | 22.7% | 25.8% | −32.0% | −31.8% | +0.67% (+0.08) |
| **B. Riley Financial** | **−7.71%** | **+2.58%** | **96.8%** | **54.2%** | **−91.3%** | **−72.2%** | **+19.15%** (+0.62) |
| Oxford Lane Capital | +6.60% | +5.51% | 8.6% | 7.5% | −11.7% | −11.6% | +1.12% (+0.38) |
| Eagle Point Credit | +1.51% | +7.03% | 14.1% | 12.7% | −21.8% | −18.6% | **−5.12%** (−0.83) |
| Babcock & Wilcox | +10.77% | +7.98% | 70.1% | 54.2% | −86.3% | −69.0% | +9.28% (+0.33) |

- Wins (preferred spread > 0): **6 / 8**, Wilson 95% **[0.41, 0.93]** — uninformative.
- **Median** pair spread: **+0.70%/yr**. The panel *mean* of +3.10% is not the typical pair.
- **Drop B. Riley** — the one issuer that went through a genuine distress event and back —
  and the pairwise spread collapses to **+0.81%/yr (t = +0.17)**.
- The B. Riley row is also a **Jensen trap**: its *arithmetic* spread is +19.15%/yr while its
  *compounded* outcome is the reverse (preferred **−7.71%/yr CAGR** vs bond **+2.58%**). A
  90%-vol crash-and-rebound inflates arithmetic means; the investor who held it lost.

## How thin is this tape? (microstructure)

$25-par preferreds and baby bonds trade by appointment. Two artefacts follow, and both
corrupt a *daily* risk comparison — a stale print (no trade, close carried forward)
**understates** vol, and bid-ask bounce (a negative lag-1 autocorrelation) **overstates** it.

| Leg | Zero-return days | Lag-1 AC | Daily-tape vol |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| **CMS-PB** (pref) | **15.5%** | **−0.28** | 24.0% |
| **OXLCZ** (bond) | **14.8%** | **−0.19** | 7.5% |
| **OXLCP** (pref) | 7.1% | **−0.28** | 8.6% |
| ECCC (bond) / ECC-PD (pref) | 6.4% / 6.1% | −0.13 / −0.07 | 12.7% / 14.1% |
| BWNB (bond) | 6.1% | +0.07 | 54.2% |
| the other ten legs | 1.5–3.5% | −0.09 … +0.08 | — |

Mean zero-day share is **5.4% (preferreds) vs 5.0% (baby bonds)** — comparable on average,
but wildly uneven name by name. **CMS-PB is the worst offender**: a 15.5% stale share and an
AC of −0.28 mean its "24.0% vol" in the per-issuer table is largely ping-pong, not risk. Its
monthly-compounded vol is **11.4%** — *below* its own baby bond's 13.5%. Any daily-frequency
risk claim on this panel has to be re-checked under compounding before it is believed.

## Is the risk step a fact or a tape artefact?

Recomputing the equal-weight ladder vol ratio and the per-pair "preferred is riskier" count
at three frequencies (gross legs, so the three rows are directly comparable):

| Frequency | n | Vol pref | Vol bond | Ratio | Preferred riskier in |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| daily | 1,105 | 18.28% | 13.93% | 1.31 | **6 / 8 pairs** |
| weekly | 231 | 21.54% | 16.56% | 1.30 | **4 / 8 pairs** |
| monthly | 53 | 22.14% | 16.99% | 1.30 | **2 / 8 pairs** |

The *panel* ratio is stable (~1.30) — but the *cross-section* is not. The count collapses
**6 → 4 → 2** as the microstructure washes out, and the two survivors are B. Riley and
Babcock & Wilcox. So the panel ratio is not eight pairs agreeing; it is two very violent
pairs dominating an equal-weight average (their monthly vols are **121%** and **88%**).

## Concentration probe — the whole study is two issuers

| Panel | n pairs | Pairwise spread (*t*) | Sharpe adv. | Vol ratio (daily / monthly) | Pref riskier (monthly) | DD pref vs bond |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **all eight** | 8 | **+3.10%** (+0.55) | +0.166 | 1.42 / 1.30 | 2 / 8 | −30.8% vs −20.4% |
| ex B. Riley | 7 | **+0.81%** (+0.17) | +0.176 | 1.30 / 1.27 | 1 / 7 | −23.1% vs −19.4% |
| **ex B. Riley + Babcock & Wilcox** | 6 | **−0.60%** (−0.21) | **−0.116** | **0.94 / 0.79** | **0 / 6** | −20.1% vs −19.3% |

This is the study's sharpest result and it kills the last standing claim. Remove the **two
distressed issuers** — which are also the only two pairs with a genuinely *wide* seniority
step — and:

- the return spread turns **negative** (−0.60%/yr, *t* = −0.21);
- the Sharpe advantage turns **negative** (−0.116);
- the vol ratio drops **below one** (0.94 daily, **0.79 monthly**) — the junior rung is the
  *calmer* one;
- the junior rung is riskier in **zero of six** pairs at monthly frequency;
- the drawdowns become indistinguishable (−20.1% vs −19.3%).

**So neither the return step nor the risk step is a seniority fact.** Both are a *distress*
fact: when an obligor's solvency is questioned, its junior rung starts behaving like equity —
which is a tautology about distress, not a measurement of what the market pays for
subordination in normal times. In the six non-distressed pairs there is no step at all, in
either direction.

## Robustness — two eras (split 2024-04-01)

| Era | n | Pref exSharpe | Bond exSharpe | Advantage | Pairwise (*t*) | Pref DD vs Bond DD |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 2022-02 → 2024-03 | 542 | −0.67 | −0.51 | **−0.16** | **−1.16%** (−0.21) | −20.6% vs −20.4% |
| 2024-04 → 2026-06 | 564 | +0.96 | +0.87 | **+0.10** | **+7.17%** (+0.72) | −30.2% vs −20.1% |

The spread **changes sign** across the halves. Neither half clears |*t*| = 1.

## Cost sensitivity (the one-way cost is a PROXY, swept 5–100 bps)

| One-way cost | Pref exSharpe | Bond exSharpe | Advantage | Ladder spread (*t*) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 5 bps | +0.376 | +0.210 | +0.166 | +4.33% (+0.65) |
| 25 bps (headline) | +0.368 | +0.202 | +0.166 | +4.29% (+0.65) |
| 100 bps | +0.339 | +0.171 | +0.167 | +4.14% (+0.62) |

Cost is almost irrelevant here — it hits both ladders alike and cancels in the spread. The
verdict is not a cost verdict.

## The dollar-neutral trade (long preferreds / short baby bonds)

Borrow on the short leg is an **ASSUMPTION**, not tape — neither rung is general-collateral
easy-to-borrow — so it is swept:

| Borrow (bp/yr) | Return | Sharpe | Vol | Max DD | HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 0 (gross) | +4.29% | +0.282 | 15.2% | −25.9% | +0.65 |
| 100 | +3.29% | +0.216 | 15.2% | −27.9% | +0.50 |
| 300 | +1.29% | +0.085 | 15.2% | −31.9% | +0.19 |

A Sharpe of 0.28 gross falling to 0.09 at a plausible hard-to-borrow rate, on a *t* of 0.65,
with a −26% drawdown. Nothing bankable.

## Does seniority pay when it should — the stress episodes

| Episode | Days | Preferred | Baby bond | Gap (pp) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 2022 rate shock (Feb–Oct 2022) | 188 | −18.68% | −18.74% | **+0.06** |
| March-2023 bank stress | 64 | +0.63% | −2.26% | **+2.89** |
| 2024 issuer stress (Feb–Sep) | 167 | +13.91% | +8.63% | **+5.28** |
| 2025 tariff shock | 82 | −10.55% | −9.51% | −1.03 |
| **COVID crash** (2-pair extension, Feb–Mar 2020) | 24 | **−10.25%** | **−19.78%** | **+9.53** |

The senior rung **failed to protect in four of five** stress windows. In the 2022 rate shock
the two rungs were indistinguishable (duration, not seniority, was the risk that mattered);
in COVID the *junior* rung fell nine points **less**, because the long-dated baby bonds were
the more rate-sensitive instrument. The thing seniority is supposed to buy is not on this tape.

## Cross-checks

- **Long-history extension** (CMS + Duke only, the two pairs with a pre-2022 tape,
  2019-04-02 → 2026-06-30, n = 1,821): pairwise spread **−0.43%/yr (*t* = −0.14)**, Sharpe
  advantage **−0.064**, vol ratio **0.95** — over seven years including COVID the seniority
  premium is *slightly negative* and the junior rung is not even the riskier one.
- **Alternative rung** (CMSA / BEPI / BIPI substituted for CMSC / BEPH / BIPH): pairwise
  **+3.84%/yr (*t* = +0.68)**, advantage +0.222, vol ratio 1.43 — the picture is not an
  artefact of which specific CUSIP we picked.
- **Survivorship probe.** The panel screens on pairs where *both* rungs are still listed in
  June 2026 — which silently deletes every redeemed bond and called preferred. The one
  redeemed pair we can still measure, **Sachem Capital (SACH-PA vs SACC, bond matured
  2024-12)**, ran the *other* way: preferred **−17.4%** cumulative vs bond **+21.6%**, a
  spread of **−10.63%/yr**. If anything the live-panel +3.10% is *flattered* by the screen.
- **Sector fallback (PFF vs the baby-bond basket), same window:** PFF excess Sharpe
  **−0.191** (CAGR −2.60%, vol 10.8%) vs the baby-bond basket **+0.202** (+1.82%, 13.3%);
  **PFF − baby bonds = −4.75%/yr (HAC *t* = −0.90)**. The *broad* preferred market **lost** to
  the senior rung over exactly the window in which our eight hand-picked preferreds won —
  another reading of how little the +3.10% means. (Correlation of our preferred ladder with
  PFF is only 0.42; the bond ladder's is 0.61.)
- **Synthetic control** (machinery proof only, never supports the stamp): on a panel with a
  *planted* +6.0%/yr junior carry premium the pairwise estimator recovers **+5.74%/yr**
  (sd 0.79%) and fires at |*t*| ≥ 2 on **20/20** seeds; on the exact null it returns
  **−0.26%/yr** (sd 0.79%) and fires on **0/20**. The estimator is powered and calibrated —
  the real-tape silence is the tape's, not the harness's.

## Verdict

- **Signal — None.** The seniority premium is **not measurable** on this tape, and neither is
  the risk step it was supposed to compensate. The pairwise
  same-issuer spread is **+3.10%/yr with HAC *t* = +0.55** and a bootstrap CI
  **[−6.80%, +13.57%]**; the Sharpe advantage **+0.166** has CI **[−0.470, +0.804]**; the
  spread **changes sign** across the two halves (−1.16% / +7.17%); it **collapses to
  +0.81%/yr (*t* = +0.17)** when B. Riley is removed and turns **negative (−0.60%/yr)** when
  Babcock & Wilcox goes too; the median pair pays **+0.70%/yr**; the seven-year two-pair
  extension is **negative** (−0.43%/yr); and the broad preferred index actually **lost**
  4.75%/yr to the baby-bond basket over the same window.
- **The risk step does not survive either — this is the audit's correction.** An earlier
  reading of this study called the risk ordering "the robust fact" on the strength of a 1.42×
  vol ratio and a 6/8 per-pair count. Both are artefacts. The 6/8 count is **daily**: it falls
  to **4/8 weekly and 2/8 monthly** as staleness and bid-ask bounce wash out (CMS-PB alone is
  15.5% stale prints with an AC of −0.28, and its 24.0% "daily vol" is 11.4% monthly — *below*
  its own bond). And the 1.42× panel ratio is not eight pairs agreeing: drop the two
  distressed issuers and it falls to **0.94 daily / 0.79 monthly**, with the junior rung
  riskier in **0 of 6** pairs and drawdowns of −20.1% vs −19.3%. The junior rung is the
  riskier one **when the issuer is in trouble**, which is a statement about distress, not
  about the price of subordination. Outside those two names there is no step in either
  direction — no premium, and nothing to pay a premium *for*.
- **Tradability — Mirage.** The dollar-neutral long-preferred / short-bond trade earns
  +4.29%/yr gross at Sharpe 0.28 on a *t* of 0.65, and decays to 0.09 at a 300 bp borrow
  assumption, with a −26% drawdown and a −91% single-name leg on the way. Cost is not the
  problem; the absence of a signal is. Neither is there a defensible *directional* tilt: over
  the longer two-pair tape the junior rung under-earned, and the screen that produced the
  positive panel number deletes exactly the pairs (redeemed bonds, distressed preferreds)
  that would run the other way.
- **Short sample, named.** Baby bonds are a young, thin, retail-distributed asset class: the
  eight-pair common window is **4.4 years**, one rate cycle and no default cycle. That, not
  a subtle estimator choice, is the binding constraint on this question.
- **The seniority step is small and uneven, named.** Only 2 of the 8 pairs are the textbook
  *perpetual preferred vs senior note*; in 4 the note is junior subordinated or perpetual, and
  in 2 the "preferred" is a dated term preferred. A question phrased as "what does the market
  pay for subordination?" is, on this panel, mostly being asked of pairs one rung apart or
  less — which is a design limit of the *listed* universe (few US issuers list both rungs at
  once), not a fixable choice.
- **The tape is thin, named.** 5.4% / 5.0% mean stale-print share, with individual legs at
  15%, and lag-1 autocorrelations to −0.28. Every risk claim is therefore stated at daily,
  weekly *and* monthly frequency; where they disagree, the daily number is the wrong one.
- **Assumptions and proxies, named.** 25 bps one-way cost (PROXY, swept 5–100 bps); short-leg
  borrow (ASSUMPTION, swept 0–300 bp/yr); Yahoo `auto_adjust` total return on thin tickers
  (PROXY); survivorship — both rungs must still be listed on 2026-06-30, and the one measurable
  redeemed pair runs −10.63%/yr the other way.
